content: Haskins Laboratories is an independent, international, and multidisciplinary research community dedicated to conducting fundamental research on spoken and written language. Established in 1935, the institution has been based in New Haven, Connecticut, since 1970. It operates as a private, non-profit research institute with a primary focus on speech, language, reading, and their biological underpinnings. Over the years, Haskins Laboratories has been at the forefront of technological and theoretical advancements, including the development of speech synthesis rules, the creation of the first functional prototype of a reading machine for the blind, and the introduction of the concept of phonemic awareness as a critical foundation for learning to read. History Since its inception, numerous researchers have contributed to groundbreaking scientific discoveries at Haskins Laboratories. These achievements owe much to the pioneering work and leadership of individuals such as Caryl Parker Haskins, Franklin S. Cooper, Alvin Liberman, Seymour Hutner, and Luigi Provasoli. The laboratory's main division, particularly since the 1940s, has been renowned for its research in speech, language, and reading. 1930s Haskins Laboratories was founded in 1935 by Caryl Haskins and Franklin S. Cooper. Initially affiliated with Harvard University, MIT, and Union College in Schenectady, NY, Caryl Haskins conducted research in microbiology, radiation physics, and other fields in Cambridge, MA, and Schenectady. In 1939, the laboratory relocated to New York City, where Seymour Hutner joined to establish a research program in microbiology, genetics, and nutrition. This program later became part of Pace University in New York. 1940s During World War II, the U.S. Office of Scientific Research and Development, under Vannevar Bush, tasked Haskins Laboratories with evaluating and developing technologies to assist blinded veterans. Alvin Liberman, an experimental psychologist, joined the laboratory to help create a sound alphabet for a reading machine for the blind. Luigi Provasoli also joined to establish a marine biology research program, which later moved to Yale University in 1970 and was disbanded upon Provasoli's retirement in 1978. 1950s Franklin S. Cooper invented the Pattern Playback, a machine that converted visual representations of speech acoustic patterns back into sound. Using this device, Alvin Liberman, Cooper, and Pierre Delattre (later joined by Katherine Safford Harris, Leigh Lisker, and others) identified the acoustic cues for perceiving phonetic segments, such as consonants and vowels. Liberman and colleagues proposed the motor theory of speech perception, hypothesizing that speech is perceived through a biological specialization—a speech module—that links articulation to its acoustic consequences. Liberman, with Frances Ingemann and others, organized these findings into a groundbreaking set of rules for speech synthesis using the Pattern Playback. 1960s Franklin S. Cooper utilized electromyographic techniques, pioneered at the University of Tokyo, to study the neuromuscular organization of speech. Leigh Lisker and Arthur Abramson investigated articulatory simplifications in voicing contrasts, demonstrating that many acoustic properties of voicing arise from variations in voice onset time. Their findings have been widely replicated and elaborated upon globally. Donald Shankweiler and Michael Studdert-Kennedy used dichotic listening techniques to show that phonetic structure, even when devoid of meaning, is an integral part of language and is typically processed in the left cerebral hemisphere. Liberman, Cooper, Shankweiler, and Studdert-Kennedy summarized 15 years of research in their influential paper, Perception of the Speech Code, which described speech as a code where speakers overlap (or coarticulate) segments to form syllables. Researchers at Haskins connected their first computer to a speech synthesizer designed by the laboratory's engineers. Ignatius Mattingly, with British collaborators, adapted the Pattern Playback rules to create the first computer program for synthesizing continuous speech from phonetically spelled input. This work advanced the development of a reading machine for the blind. 1970s In 1970, Haskins Laboratories relocated to New Haven, Connecticut, and established affiliations with Yale University and the University of Connecticut. Isabelle Liberman, Donald Shankweiler, Alvin Liberman, and Ignatius Mattingly studied the relationship between speech perception and reading, leading to the development of the concept of phonemic awareness. This concept, central to the alphabetic principle, remains a cornerstone of the laboratory's current reading pedagogy program. Patrick Nye led a team working on the reading machine for the blind, culminating in the creation of the first automatic text-to-speech reading machine. By the end of the decade, commercial entities began designing and manufacturing reading machines for the blind. In 1973, Franklin S. Cooper was selected to investigate the infamous 18-minute gap in President Richard Nixon's White House tapes related to the Watergate scandal. Building on earlier work, Philip Rubin developed the sinewave synthesis program, which demonstrated that listeners could perceive continuous speech without traditional speech cues, paving the way for a dynamic view of speech as trajectories through articulatory-acoustic space. Rubin and colleagues also developed the first articulatory synthesizer controlled in a physically meaningful way for interactive experiments. 1980s Studies of various writing systems supported the hypothesis that all reading activates the phonological form of a word before or simultaneously with its meaning. Researchers, including George Lukatela, Michael Turvey, Leonard Katz, Ram Frost, Laurie Feldman, and Shlomo Bentin, conducted experiments in multiple languages. Carol Fowler proposed the direct realism theory of speech perception, suggesting that listeners perceive gestures directly from the acoustic signal. J. A. Scott Kelso and colleagues demonstrated functional synergies in speech gestures experimentally. Elliot Saltzman developed a dynamical systems theory of synergistic action and implemented it as a working model of speech production. Linguists Catherine Browman and Louis Goldstein introduced the theory of articulatory phonology, where gestures are the fundamental units of both phonetic action and phonological knowledge. These models were integrated into a gestural computational model of speech production. Saltzman and Rubin initiated the IS group to explore cutting-edge developments in science and technology and foster interdisciplinary collaboration. 1990s Katherine Safford Harris, Frederica Bell-Berti, and colleagues studied the phasing and cohesion of articulatory speech gestures. Kenneth Pugh was among the first to use functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to study brain activity associated with reading and reading disabilities. Pugh, Donald Shankweiler, Weija Ni, Einar Mencl, and colleagues developed novel neuroimaging applications to measure brain activity during sentence comprehension. Philip Rubin, Louis Goldstein, and Mark Tiede designed the Configurable Articulatory Synthesizer (CASY), a 3D model of the vocal tract that replicates MRI images of actual speakers. Researchers extended this work to study the relationship between speech production and perception. Shankweiler, Susan Brady, Anne Fowler, and others investigated whether poor readers' weak memory and perception were specifically tied to phonological deficits, rejecting broader cognitive deficits as the cause of reading difficulties. 2000s Anne Fowler and Susan Brady launched the Early Reading Success (ERS) program, part of the Haskins Literacy Initiative, to promote evidence-based reading instruction. The ERS program demonstrated the efficacy of professional development in reading instruction for teachers of children in kindergarten through second grade. The Mastering Reading Instruction program continued this work, combining professional development with Haskins-trained mentors. David Ostry and colleagues explored the neurological basis of motor control using a robot arm to influence jaw movement. Douglas Whalen and Khalil Iskarous pioneered the use of ultrasound and Optotrak technology to monitor articulators during speech production. Donald Shankweiler and David Braze developed an eye movement laboratory to investigate reading processes in normal and disabled readers by combining eye-tracking data with brain activity measures. In March 2005, Haskins Laboratories moved to a new state-of-the-art facility on George Street in New Haven.
